entities.name: Ottoman–Venetian War of 1570–1573
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Ottoman–Venetian War of 1570–1573 was a pivotal conflict between the Ottoman Empire and the Holy League from 1570 to 1573, taking place in Cyprus and marking a significant turning point in the struggle for control of the Eastern Mediterranean.

The war began on July 7, 1570, when the Ottoman Empire, under the leadership of Sultan Selim II, launched a massive invasion of Cyprus, which was a strategic outpost of the Venetian Republic. The Ottomans, bolstered by their naval superiority and the support of the local Muslim population, quickly overwhelmed the Venetian forces, capturing key cities such as Nicosia and Famagusta. The war ended on January 12, 1573, with the signing of the Treaty of Constantinople, which ceded Cyprus to the Ottoman Empire and marked the beginning of a long period of Ottoman dominance in the region.

The Ottoman–Venetian War of 1570–1573 had significant consequences for the balance of power in the Eastern Mediterranean and the fate of the Venetian Republic. The war marked a major defeat for the Venetians, who never fully recovered from the loss of their strategic outpost in Cyprus. The war also had a profound impact on the development of the Ottoman Empire, which continued to expand its territories in the region and establish itself as a major world power.

The war also saw the emergence of a new generation of Ottoman leaders, including the young Sultan Selim II, who would go on to play a major role in shaping the future of the empire. The war's legacy can be seen in the continued Ottoman dominance of the region for centuries to come, as well as the eventual rise of the Ottoman Empire as a major world power.
